transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-12
Start time: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (NimbleHealth - ML Eng), Maya Patel (NimbleHealth - Product), Sam Ortega (NimbleHealth - Security)

Summary:
Quick weekly POC sync to review quality eval results from last run, discuss prompt-set tuning and regression detection, and agree next steps for guardrails and security checklist. SE ran targeted evals on 500 samples; plan to expand to 1k. Some regression signals on finance-related prompts (higher hallucination), discussing prompt templates and fallback policies.

Topics:
- Eval results and scoring methodology (preference vs automated metrics)
- Prompt set updates and prompt engineering best practices
- Guardrails and safety: filters, hallucination detection, post-processing
- Deployment variant discussion: host vs dedicated for latency/cost tradeoffs
- Next steps / action items

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: All right, hey everyone thanks for joining, um this is our weekly POC sync. Alex from Redwood here, I think we have Priya from the SE team and then Jordan, Maya, Sam from NimbleHealth. quick check on audio?
[00:06] Jordan: yeah good to go, thanks Alex.
[00:08] Maya: good here.
[00:10] Priya: all good.
[00:12] Alex: cool, i'll kick us off. Priya ran the latest eval over the last set of prompts, 500 examples, maybe Priya can summarize high level.
[00:20] Priya: sure, so we ran the scoring harness against the 500-sample production-ish set you shared, jordan. We used a mixed scoring approach: pairwise preference for the top-100 human-eval subset and automated heuristics (hallucination signal, slot fill accuracy, and a simple n-gram overlap for factual queries) for the rest. Overall preference win-rate for the tuned prompt set is about 68% vs the baseline, but we did see regressions on two families: finance statements and prior-auth medical claims where the model hallucinated numbers.
[00:48] Jordan: yeah that lines up with what we've been seeing in staging — the model tends to invent invoice totals when prompts reference previous invoices.
[00:56] Maya: can you clarify "preference win-rate" quick? we talk to product folks but i want to make sure team knows.
[01:04] Priya: totally — so for the 100 human-labeled items we ran A/B style preference tests where reviewers chose which completion was better; the tuned prompts won 68 of 100. It's noisy but directional. The automated metrics show a smaller lift, around 6-8% on slot accuracy.
[01:20] Sam: when you say hallucination signal, is that the external QA step or something inside Redwood Optimize?
[01:26] Priya: it's a lightweight QA post-check we run in the harness — some rule-based checks for numeric consistency and a second-pass retriever to look for supporting evidence. we don't rely on a full external retriever in this run, which is why some cases slipped through.
[01:38] Alex: also to call out, we had KV cache and batching configured differently during the test which reduced tail latency but might have affected context window behavior — Priya?
[01:48] Priya: right, we applied more aggressive batching to hit your latency targets in the Dedicated sim, that means the runtime compaction changed how long term context was preserved for certain sessions; could explain a little of the regression for invoices that need full prior conversation context.
[02:02] Jordan: ok that makes sense. so what's the plan to reduce the hallucinations? is it more prompt engineering, more retrieval, or guardrails?
[02:12] Priya: a mix — immediate: refine prompt templates to make numeric constraints explicit and add guardrail filters to detect invented totals. mid-term: run the 1k eval batch with the retriever enabled for risky categories, and tune the fallback policy to return "unable to confirm" rather than a guessed value.
[02:28] Maya: do we have an estimate on SLO impact if we enable retriever for those categories?
[02:34] Alex: preliminary numbers — enabling retriever for ~10% of traffic increases p50 latency by ~80-120ms on Dedicated, cost delta modest but visible; we can route those to Dedicated/Private if you want strict latency control.
[02:45] Sam: from a security perspective, will the retriever require additional data access? we need to ensure it doesn't expose PHI and it obeys our KMS rules.
[02:54] Priya: for the POC we used a sandboxed retriever against synthetic data, but for production we'd integrate with your vault or read-only search with RBAC. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and we can instrument audit logs — we'll provide the SOC2 artifact.
[03:08] Sam: ok please send the SOC2 link.
[03:11] Alex: noted, will add to action items.
[03:13] Priya: i also want to mention regression detection: we added a lightweight drift monitor that flags a 5% drop in preference win-rate on a per-prompt-family basis and a 10% jump in hallucination signals. We saw one flag this week on the "billing/invoice" family.
[03:28] Jordan: is that historical? can we see the time series?
[03:31] Priya: yes, we've uploaded a snapshot to the shared spreadsheet (link posted in chat). the time series is rough but you can see the uptick starting last Thursday after the prompt orthogonalization change.
[03:43] Maya: orthogonalization change = which change?
[03:45] Priya: we changed the instruction phrasing to try to reduce verbosity, that inadvertently loosened the numeric constraint so the model sometimes dropped qualifiers.
[03:54] Alex: classic. we can revert or patch the prompt. which do you prefer, jordan?
[03:59] Jordan: let's patch the prompt first and re-run the 1k eval; if it doesn't move the needle we'll consider retriever fallback.
[04:06] Priya: ok i'll draft two prompt variants (tight-numeric and explicit-guard) and run both. i'll add a post-processing filter to catch numbers that don't match earlier context.
[04:16] Sam: post-processing filter — will that run in the runtime or offline? we prefer runtime for security but it's heavier.
[04:22] Priya: we can do it at runtime as a lightweight regex-and-lookup step or as async post-check that triggers a follow-up clarifying question. tradeoff is latency vs user experience.
[04:33] Alex: also want to talk about scoring: we used pairwise human evals but to catch regressions earlier we recommend adding automated synthetic tests for the top 20 prompt families and gating deploys if hallucination signal > threshold.
[04:47] Jordan: how easy is that to integrate in our CI?
[04:50] Priya: pretty straightforward — we can provide a small test harness that runs locally or in CI. it hits the same scoring functions we used and outputs a pass/fail.
[04:58] Maya: can you show a sample output?
[05:00] Priya: yes i'll attach the CSV and gist after the call. it includes per-prompt-family metrics: preference win-rate, hallucination rate, slot accuracy, and a derived quality score.
[05:12] Alex: on routing and deployment — if you want strict isolation and predictable latency for retriever-enabled flows we recommend routing those requests to Redwood Dedicated or Redwood Private; Hosted is fine for lower-sensitivity flows.
[05:26] Jordan: cost-wise what's the delta for Dedicated?
[05:29] Alex: we'll send updated pricing but rough ballpark for this pilot is a 20-30% premium over hosted for guaranteed capacity; depends on commit and burst options. we'll follow up with a SOW.
[05:41] Sam: also need to confirm data residency and retention settings for the pilot. do you support configurable retention?
[05:47] Priya: yes, retention is configurable per-customer; for POC we used 30-day retention but production can be set to shorter windows or disabled with Private deployment.
[05:57] Maya: quick question on guardrails — can we enforce an "unable to confirm" fallback automatically? we don't want an agent guessing.
[06:05] Priya: yes we have automatic fallback policies — rule-based or learned threshold — that can return a structured response like {status: unable_to_confirm} and prompt a clarifying question. in transcripts the JSON got garbled so sorry if that showed up odd in the doc.
[06:20] Jordan: that's good. what's the testing cadence you recommend? weekly runs?
[06:24] Priya: weekly for the first month, then move to biweekly once stability's confirmed. also run targeted runs after any prompt/rollout changes.
[06:33] Alex: ok let's capture next steps. Priya, you'll run the 1k eval with retriever enabled for risky categories and two prompt variants — tight-numeric and explicit-guard — due 2025-02-19.
[06:44] Priya: yep.
[06:46] Alex: Jordan - you'll gather 200 labeled fail-cases and staging access, due 2025-02-20.
[06:52] Jordan: will do.
[06:53] Alex: Sam - you'll send SOC2 cert and the compliance Qs by 2025-02-15.
[06:58] Sam: yes, i'll pull and send the docs.
[07:00] Alex: i'll send the Dedicated pricing and pilot SOW by 2025-02-14.
[07:04] Maya: thanks.
[07:06] Priya: one more item, i'll also add the synthetic CI test harness to the repo and give you usage notes.
[07:13] Alex: perfect. any other questions?
[07:15] Maya: none from product.
[07:16] Jordan: all set.
[07:17] Sam: good.
[07:18] Alex: great, we'll follow up in the thread with the links, spreadsheet and the updated prompts. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

References/links mentioned: shared spreadsheet (link posted in chat), sample CSV/gist (to be attached by Priya), SOC2 artifact (to be sent by Alex/Sam).

Action items (as read out):
- Priya: run 1k eval with retriever enabled; test two prompt variants; deliver results by 2025-02-19.
- Alex: share Dedicated pricing and pilot SOW by 2025-02-14 and SOC2 link.
- Jordan: provide 200 labeled fail-cases and staging access by 2025-02-20.
- Sam: send SOC2 cert and compliance Qs by 2025-02-15.

End file."
